title: ABCD SYNDROME
alt_titles: ALBINISM, BLACK LOCK, CELL MIGRATION DISORDER OF THE NEUROCYTES OF THE GUT, AND DEAFNESS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is caused by a homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.

paragraphs.text: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive neural crest disorder characterized by albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease), and deafness (Gross et al., 1995; Verheij et al., 2002). Verheij et al. (2002) noted that the phenotype clearly overlaps with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome, and suggested that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Gross et al. (1995) reported a macrosomic newborn girl, the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents, with albinism, a black lock at the right temporo-occipital region, and retinal depigmentation. Bilateral deafness was confirmed by brainstem auditory-evoked potentials. She also had a severe defect of intestinal innervation: biopsy showed aganglionosis of the large intestine and total absence of neurocytes and nerve fibers in the small intestine, indicating a total lack of sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation. She died of intestinal dysfunction at 5 weeks. Four sibs had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth; the other 9 sibs were well, with an unremarkable phenotype. The authors considered the association of albinism, black lock, deafness, and total lack of intestinal neural innervation to represent a new neural crest syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Gross et al. (1995) proposed autosomal recessive inheritance of ABCD syndrome on the basis of a family in which 5 children of consanguineous Kurdish parents were affected. Verheij et al. (2002) found a homozygous EDNRB mutation in the index patient of this family, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.evidence_quote: She was the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents. Four sibs of our patient had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth.
checks.explanation: The index girl plus 4 affected sibs makes 5 affected children of consanguineous Kurdish parents.

paragraphs.text: Because the features of ABCD syndrome overlap with those of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (sensorineural deafness; hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and irides; and Hirschsprung disease), Verheij et al. (2002) screened DNA of the index patient of the ABCD syndrome family reported by Gross et al. (1995) for mutations in the endothelin B receptor gene (EDNRB), a gene known to be involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome. They identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 of EDNRB (R201X). They suggested that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

agent.process_note: I read all three files in full. Gross et al. (1995) and Verheij et al. (2002) are abstracts only, and Witkop (1979) is a title only with no usable content, so I did not cite it. The reference data gave no MIM number or chromosomal location for EDNRB, so I left both out of the intro. The Verheij abstract gives only the protein change (R201X), not the nucleotide change. It also does not report whether the parents or affected sibs were tested for segregation, or any functional studies, so those details are missing from the entry.
